fields.title: Stapel: Everything is 'Done', Demo Tomorrow
fields.summary: Tasks are closed, the team is happy, but the last identical release fell apart after a week. Decide how to accept the work.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do two days before the release?
fields.brief/company: Stapel is a fictional order management service for furniture manufacturing. Clients are 40 small workshops. Team: five developers, one QA engineer, and you.
fields.brief/context: The sprint is over, all eight tasks are in the 'Done' column. Demo is tomorrow, release is the day after. The last release looked the same, and we had to roll it back a week later: some screens wouldn't open in workshops with a high volume of orders.
fields.brief/objective: Avoid releasing a second consecutive update that has to be rolled back.
fields.brief/constraints: One day until the demo and two until the release. Moving the release is possible, but it would be the second consecutive delay.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you will do in the remaining two days and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A post-mortem takeaway that doesn't make it into a checklist, Definition of Done, or test lives only until the next crunch. The difference between 'we agreed to test on real volumes' and a single line in the shared Definition of Done is the difference between repeating a mistake and avoiding it. Also, acceptance should not be run by the person who built it: the author unconsciously bypasses weak spots, even when honestly trying to show them.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Eight tasks. The main one is 'weekly workshop load plan': a screen where the foreman sees which orders are scheduled for which day.

Each task is marked as 'done' in the tracker. What this actually means varies by developer: two have automated tests, the others don't; three tested on their local machines, two on the test environment.

The team has no shared Definition of Done. At the last demo, a debate on whether a task is considered done without testing on large volumes took half an hour and ended in nothing.

The 'load plan' task was discussed once, verbally, for ten minutes. The tracker card has just two lines.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Test environment: one workshop, 30 orders, 4 foremen.

Reality: median workshop has 180 orders per week; the three largest clients have 900+. This is exactly where the last release broke.

QA engineer: 'Tomorrow, I can run a large client's export through the new load plan screen. That will take half a day. But then I won't have time to run the other seven tasks even through the happy path.'

The production data export is anonymized and has been available since the last post-mortem.

The developer who built the load plan: 'I didn't test on 900 orders. I don't think it's fundamentally different.'
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
34 support tickets in a month, 19 of which are the exact same question: 'how to cancel an order that is already in progress'. Cancellation exists in the product, but it is hidden in the card menu.

Last time, this was addressed with an article in the knowledge base. Tickets after publication: 19 in the previous month, 19 in this one.

Foremen in workshops are people who open the product between operations, often wearing gloves, on a tablet.

The Commercial Director expects the release to increase the share of workshops that manage their plan in the product rather than on paper. Currently, it is 22%. What growth to consider a success has not been formulated.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The developer ran the demo: showed it on the test environment, everything worked.

Six days after the release, three large clients reported that the orders screen wouldn't open. The reason was a query that ran instantly on 30 orders but hit a timeout on 900.

The rollback took a day; it took a month to rebuild trust with two of the three clients.

During the post-mortem, we agreed to 'test on real volumes next time'. This was never written down in any checklist—the agreement remained verbal.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Accept it yourself based on requirements and production data
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Give the QA engineer a day to run the load plan against a large client's export, test the other tasks yourself based on the documented requirements, and add the agreement from the last post-mortem to the shared Definition of Done checklist. Define success criteria before the release.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The QA engineer runs the load plan on an export of 900 orders: the screen takes 14 seconds to open. The reason is the same as last time—a query without a limit. The developer fixes it in half a day.
You test the other seven tasks yourself based on the requirements in the cards. Two tasks fail: one didn't account for canceled orders, which is caught before the demo, not during it.
The team adds a single line to the Definition of Done checklist: 'tested on a client export of at least 500 orders'. This line appears once and applies to all tasks.
Before the release, success is defined: the share of workshops managing their plan in the product will grow from 22% to 30% in a month, and the share of cancellation tickets will not increase.
The release goes out the day after tomorrow and is not rolled back.
Trade-off: the demo goes ahead without a full walkthrough of the seven tasks, and you don't address the 19 support tickets in this release.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Run the demo as usual and release
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: All tasks are in 'Done', the team worked for two weeks. Show them at the demo and release the day after tomorrow as planned.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The demo goes smoothly: the developer walks through the test environment, everything worked.
Five days after the release, two large clients report that the load plan won't open. The reason is the same query without a limit as last time.
Rollback, the second one in two months. During the post-mortem, 'we need to test on real volumes' is voiced again.
The Commercial Director asks what has changed since the last post-mortem. There is no answer: the agreement was verbal and never documented.
Trade-off: you saved two days and repeated a mistake whose cause was known and documented in your own post-mortem.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Focus on instructions for the foremen
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Nineteen support tickets a month about the same thing is the most visible user pain point. Spend two days on clear instructions and onboarding tooltips.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The instructions are ready for the release. Tickets next month: 18.
The reason is that a knowledge base article was already written last time with the same result: a foreman looks for answers on the screen in gloves between operations, not in the help section.
The load plan is released without volume testing. A week later, a large client reports that the screen won't open.
Trade-off: you addressed real user pain using a method that was already proven ineffective, and ignored a risk that had already caused a rollback once.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Postpone the release and cover everything with test cases
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The root cause is that 'Done' means different things. Postpone the release by a week, write test cases for all eight tasks, and accept them only based on those cases.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
A week is spent on test cases. This results in 60 cases, which indeed find four defects, including the high-volume issue.
Price: the second consecutive delay, and the Commercial Director asks why releases are now coming out once every month and a half.
For the next sprint, the team writes test cases in much less detail—maintaining sixty cases turned out to be unsustainable.
Trade-off: you found the defects but paid with a week's delay and a second postponement, where a single run on production data and a single line in the shared Definition of Done would have sufficed.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The queue is not ordered: priority is set by labels rather than sequentially
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The task went into progress without a discussion, and the discrepancy surfaced during acceptance
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The deviation from the plan was visible days in advance, but no one called it out
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: The bottleneck in the flow is not identified: they look at busyness rather than task age
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: The definition of 'Done' is understood differently; the team has no shared minimum standard
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Acceptance is done by showing the happy path on test data
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: A recurring issue is addressed with text instead of removing the root cause
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: Release success is defined after the fact based on a rising chart
